background.definition: Vitiligo is an acquired pigmentary disorder in which patients present with chalk-white or milk-white macules or patches. Melanocytes are usually absent from these lesions. Segmental vitiligo typically has unilateral cutaneous involvement in a dermatomal or quasi-dermatomal distribution and is more difficult to treat than nonsegmental vitiligo. The nonsegmental type is subdivided into generalized vitiligo (most common, with widely distributed, scattered patches), focal vitiligo (one or more macules in a single area in a nondermatomal distribution), and universal vitiligo (total or subtotal cutaneous depigmentation).

list.listitem: Between 1% and 2% of the population is affected with vitiligo.
There is a bimodal pattern of onset ,first in childhood and then in adulthood. Two-thirds of cases happen in adulthood.
The natural progression can be unpredictable as it ranges from insidious to rapid in onset.
Vitiligo is more striking in individuals with darker complexions, but disease prevalence is actually no different among races; it also occurs equally in men and women.
See Pathophysiology section.

Sites of repeated trauma or friction are more prone to the development of vitiligo, an occurrence called Koebner's phenomenon. Sources include bony prominences, clothing, surrounding skin (eg, skin folds), or other objects.
The pathophysiology is as yet undetermined, but there are several hypotheses.
Autoimmune hypothesis (most likely): cellular and/or humoral autoimmune destruction of melanocytes.
Oxidative stress hypothesis: significantly elevated concentration of hydrogen peroxide disrupts functioning of epidermal melanocytes.
Neural hypothesis: chemical mediators released from peripheral nerve endings cause melanocyte dysfunction and/or destruction (more likely for segmental vitiligo).
Convergence theory: interplay of multiple mechanisms in disease development.
Melanocytorrhagic theory: intrinsic cell-cell adhesion defects make melanocytes more susceptible to detachment after autoimmune, neural, oxidative, and/or physical insults.
Diagnosis is primarily based on the clinical impression of oval, depigmented macules or patches of varying sizes with scalloped margins. C
The Wood's lamp may be a useful diagnostic tool in visualizing depigmented macules that may not be visible with the naked eye. C
Biopsies may be useful in ruling out an alternative diagnosis but are of limited utility in diagnosing vitiligo. C

list.listitem: Although onset has been observed in all age groups, 50% of those affected first develop depigmented macules before the age of 18.

Vitiligo is characterized by chalk-white or milk-white macules or patches. Lesions are usually round to oval in shape but are occasionally linear. The patches often coalesce, forming larger, nongeometric shapes. The borders are usually scalloped, with fairly distinct to slightly brushed margins.

The diameters of the lesions range from several millimeters to many centimeters, and there may be a large degree of variability among lesions even within the same individual. Poliosis (hair depigmentation) is often observed.
The typical vitiligo lesion lacks cutaneous changes other than depigmentation.
See "Approach to the Patient" for definition of different classes of vitiligo, which guides treatment.
With nonsegmental vitiligo, new lesions can appear throughout life in an unpredictable manner.

A Wood's lamp can be helpful in detecting depigmented macules in lighter skin types or in sun-protected areas in all but the darkest skin. The procedure is performed by shining the lamp on suspicious lesions in a room that is as dark as possible. Under the Wood's lamp, bright white or blue-white macules are the most consistent with vitiligo.

In patients with atypical presentations, a skin biopsy may be helpful. Typically, established vitiligo macules show normal skin except for an absence of melanocytes. However, this is not diagnostic of vitiligo. Melanocytes may be present in vitiligo lesions in some cases. The skin biopsy may be most useful in ruling out an alternative diagnosis.

Because of frequent association of vitiligo with autoimmune thyroiditis, obtain thyroid-stimulating hormone level and antithyroid antibodies. Because of the less frequent associations with diabetes mellitus type I, pernicious anemia, and Addison's disease, obtain fasting blood glucose, CBC, and/or adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test only if clinically indicated.
Suspect vitiligo in the patient presenting with oval, depigmented macules and patches of varying sizes with scalloped margins. No cutaneous changes should be present other than depigmentation.

Diagnostic testing or biopsy is not typically required for diagnosis. Laboratory testing may be useful in diagnosing any associated comorbidities. Wood's lamp can be helpful in detecting depigmented macules.
Treatment is based on classification as segmental or nonsegmental vitiligo and its subgroups (see Definition).
Segmental vitiligo anywhere and nonsegmental vitiligo lesions located on the lips, hands, feet, fingers, and genitalia are the least responsive to medical therapy. C

Localized vitiligo in adults is best initially managed with topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus 0.1% BID) for lesions on the head and neck and topical corticosteroids for lesions on the trunk and extremities. Targeted narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy can be used as second-line therapy.B
Topical ruxolitinib results in greater response than vehicle (29.8% vs 7.4%, p < 0.001, NNT = 5) but causes acne and pruritus at the application site. B
Generalized depigmentation in adults is best managed with NB-UVB phototherapy. B
Autologous skin transplantation is most successful in children and adults with stable segmental vitiligo and adults with stable localized nonsegmental vitiligo. B

Localized vitiligo in adults is best initially managed with topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus 0.1% BID) for lesions on the head and neck and topical corticosteroids for lesions on the trunk and extremities.

A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence from small, individual studies of existing treatments for vitiligo but the generazability and applicability of these findings are limited by the varying study designs and measured outcomes, and paucity of quality of life outcomes. Studies that evaluate durability of repigmentation and well-designed RCTs meauring standard outcomes and quality of life measures are needed.
Topical tacrolimus has been shown to improve narrowband UVB-induced repigmentation.

A randomized double-blind study showed twice weekly 0.1% tacrolimus ointment is effective maintenance therapy in previously successfully repigmented vitiligo. Sixteen patients with 31 patches in placebo group versus 19 patients with 41 patches in the tacrolimus group showed 40% of lesions had some depigmentation in the placebo group compared to 9.7% in the tacrolimus group (p = 0.0075).

Two Phase 3 trials randomized a total of 674 patients to topical ruxolitinib 1.5% twice daily or vehicle control for 24 weeks. Ruxolitinib (Opzelura) resulted in a greater response than vehicle (29.8% vs 7.4%, p < 0.001, NNT = 5) but can cause acne and pruritus at the application site.

An RCT of 364 patients with active nonsegmental vitiligo demonstrated the efficacy and safety of oral ritlecitinib (JAK/TEC inhibitor) over placebo at 24 and 48 weeks, as measured by percent change from baseline in Facial-Vitiligo Area Scoring Index. However, more studies are needed, especially those measuring permanence of repigmentation and quality of life measures, before systemic immunotherapy can be routinely recommended. Adding narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) to ritlecitinib may improve outcomes, but larger trials are needed to confirm this.

Medical depigmentation can be considered in patients with vitiligo involving >50% BSA or on exposed areas, like the hands and face, which have been resistant to other treatments. This can be accomplished using monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, laser therapy, or cryotherapy.

Cosmetic cover-up is an option to camouflage depigmented areas, although it may come off with sweating or direct physical contact. Manual tattooing of amelanotic macules may be considered, but color matching may be difficult. Use of sunscreens is recommended but has not been well studied.
Methods of skin graft procurement include minigrafting, dermabrasion followed by split-skin graft, and suction-blister epidermal grafting for direct or post-culture transplantation.

A meta-analysis of 117 studies found the following rates of at least 90% repigmentation with different surgical procedures: punch grafting 46%, thin skin grafting 72%, suction blister grafting 62%, noncultured epidermal cell suspension 48%, noncultured follicular cell suspension 36%, and cultured epidermal cell suspension 57%.
Antioxidants such as polypodium leucotomos, lipoic acid, vitamins C and E, and polyunsaturated fatty acids may increase repigmentation induced with NB-UVB phtotherapy.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with 47 participants with active vitiligo, spread of vitligo ceased in 80% and 36% (p-value of 0.006) patients given gingko biloba 40 mg TID vs placebo, respectively.

A meta-analysis of twenty-two studies totalling 1448 patients with vitiligo found significantly higher serum homocysteine levels (SMD 0.550, 95% CI 0.262-0.838) and lower B12 levels than controls (SMD 0.430, 95% CI -0.738 to -0.121).

In a randomized double-blind trial involving 56 patients with nonsegmental vitiligo, greater than 50% improvement in body surface area affected was experienced by 64% of patients in the narrowband UVB group compared with 36% of the PUVA group.
For focal vitiligo resistant to topical treatment, targeted phototherapy can be utilized. The 308nm excimer light is superior to targeted NB-UVB.
Generalized depigmentation in adults is best managed with narrowband UVB phototherapy for 6 to 12 months.

A systematic review of 35 studies identified 29 studies of narrowband UVB and found at least a mild response in 62% at 3 months and 75% at 12 months; a marked response occurred in 13% at 3 months, and 36% at 12 months. In 9 studies of psoralen UVA phototherapy, at least a mild reponse was reported in approximately half of patients at 6 months and 62% at 12 months.
Topical corticosteroids combined with home-based narrow band UVB was safe and effective in a randomized trial of 517 patients.
Vitiligo can be associated with substantial psychosocial morbidity. Patients should be informed about vitligo support groups/organizations and when appropriate, referred for psychotherapy. C
With nonsegmental vitiligo, new lesions can appear throughout life in an unpredictable manner. C
Segmental vitiligo usually spreads rapidly initially and then stabilizes within 1 year of onset. B
Medical treatment of vitiligo in children is similar to adults.

The Pediatric Dermatology Research Alliance Consensus Guidelines have found evidence supporting the use of topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and topical Janus-associated kinase (JAK) inhibitors for the treatment of vitiligo in children, adolescent, and young adults. The choice of treatment is influenced by patient's age, body location, and extent of body surface area involvement.
Children with stable segmental vitiligo have been successfully treated with a cellular subtype of autologous skin transplantation.
